market_context: United States; fresh and unsweetened dried fruit
title: Fresh fruit vs. dried fruit: sugar, fiber, and calories

seo.title: Fresh vs. dried fruit: sugar, fiber, and calories
seo.meta_description: Dried fruit concentrates sugar, fiber and calories as water is removed. Raisins are about 299 kcal/100 g versus about 69 kcal/100 g for grapes.
seo.search_intent: Compare fresh and dried fruit for sugar, fiber, calories, serving size and overall nutrition.

excerpt: Dried fruit does not automatically gain sugar; removing water concentrates what was already in the fruit. Raisins provide roughly 299 kcal and 59 g sugar per 100 g, compared with about 69 kcal and 15.5 g sugar in fresh grapes. Fiber and minerals are concentrated too, but a calorie-dense portion is much easier to eat quickly.
content_html:
A grape and a raisin come from the same fruit, but they do not contain the same amount of water. Once much of that water is removed, nutrients and calories become much more concentrated by weight.

The per-100-g comparison changes dramatically

Fresh grapes provide about 69 kcal, 18 g carbohydrate, 15.5 g sugar and 0.9 g fiber per 100 g. Seedless raisins provide roughly 299 kcal, 79 g carbohydrate, 59 g sugar and 3.7 g fiber per 100 g.

The raisin did not manufacture four times as much sugar. A 100 g pile of raisins represents many more original grapes because much of their water has been removed. Comparing equal weights therefore compares a water-rich food with a concentrated one.

Fiber becomes concentrated too

The same concentration applies to fiber. In the grape-raisin example, fiber rises from about 0.9 g/100 g to 3.7 g/100 g. Minerals such as potassium and iron can also become more concentrated by weight.

Some vitamins are more vulnerable to processing and storage. Vitamin C, for example, can decline during drying, so dried fruit is not simply an identical miniature version of fresh fruit.

Serving size changes the practical picture

People rarely eat 100 g of raisins the way they might eat 100 g of grapes. A roughly 30 g serving of raisins provides about 90 kcal, while 100 g of grapes provides around 69 kcal. The gap per realistic serving is much smaller than the per-100-g comparison suggests.

The practical issue is how easy dried fruit is to eat quickly. Thirty grams takes little space and only a few bites, while the same calories in fresh fruit usually come with more water and volume.

What about added sugar?

Plain dried fruit can contain only the fruit's naturally occurring sugars. But products such as dried cranberries, mango or pineapple may contain added sugar. In those products, the higher sugar content is not only a result of water removal.

The ingredient list settles the question. If sugar, syrup, glucose or another sweetener appears in addition to the fruit, the product is different from simply dried fruit.

Which is more filling?

Fresh fruit generally supplies much more water and physical volume per calorie. That tends to make a given amount of energy take up more space in a bowl and in the stomach. Dried fruit still contains fiber, but its energy density is far greater: in the grape-raisin example, 299 kcal/100 g versus 69 kcal/100 g.

The useful takeaway

Dried fruit can be nutritious and convenient in yogurt, cereal or trail mixes. Treat it as a concentrated food: use smaller portions, check for added sugar and do not assume that 100 g of dried fruit represents the same amount of food as 100 g fresh.

faq.question: Does dried fruit have more sugar than fresh fruit?
faq.answer: Per 100 g, yes, because water removal concentrates the natural sugar. Raisins contain about 59 g sugar per 100 g versus about 15.5 g in fresh grapes.

faq.question: Does dried fruit still contain fiber?
faq.answer: Yes. Fiber becomes concentrated by weight; raisins provide roughly 3.7 g/100 g compared with about 0.9 g/100 g in grapes.

faq.question: Does all dried fruit contain added sugar?
faq.answer: No. Some products contain only fruit, while others such as certain dried cranberries, mangoes or pineapples may have added sweeteners. Check the ingredient list.
